scenes.title: Chatbot. Assistant. AI employee.
scenes.subtitle: Three words vendors use as if they mean the same thing.
scenes.narration: Chatbot. Assistant. AI employee. Vendors use all three words like they mean the same thing. They don't.

scenes.title: A bell on the counter

items.label: You ring it
items.text: It reads out the opening hours

items.label: Words in, words out
items.text: No access to your systems

scenes.narration: A chatbot is a bell on the counter. You ring it, and a recorded voice reads out the opening hours. Words in, words out. Useful, but that's all it does.

scenes.title: A helpful stranger

items.label: Great answers
items.text: Drafts, summaries, explanations

items.label: Doesn't work here
items.text: You copy the result into the real system yourself

scenes.narration: An assistant is a helpful stranger in the waiting room. Great answers, but they don't work here. You still copy the result into the real system yourself.

scenes.title: A colleague at the desk

items.label: A role
items.text: A job, not just a prompt

items.label: A procedure you can read
items.text: Steps you can open and change

items.label: Works in your systems
items.text: Looks up and updates real records

items.label: A manager
items.text: A person in your company supervises it

scenes.narration: An AI employee is the colleague at the desk. It has a role. It follows a procedure you can read. It works inside your systems. And a person in your company is in charge of it.

scenes.title: What happens after the answer?
scenes.narration: Here's the test. Ask what happens after the answer. Does it act in your systems? Does it follow your procedure? Does it leave a record? And who answers for it?

scenes.title: It doesn't ask first by default

items.label: In Wetel today
items.text: An agent pauses only where you add an approval step

scenes.narration: One honest gap. In Wetel, an AI employee does not ask first by default. It pauses only where you add an approval step.

scenes.title: One job. One procedure. One named person.
scenes.subtitle: wetel.dev
scenes.narration: So start small. Pick one job. Write down the steps. Name the person in charge. The full guide is on wetel dot dev.

title: What if nobody approves in time?

scenes.title: The manager is on holiday. Now what?
scenes.subtitle: Your AI employee asked for approval. Nobody answered.
scenes.narration: Your AI employee asked a manager for approval before doing something risky. The manager is on holiday. Now what?

scenes.title: An approval is a step you add

items.label: Run pauses
items.text: Until a workspace owner decides

items.label: Owner is notified
items.text: In the app, with an approvals inbox

items.label: Not automatic
items.text: Nothing pauses unless you add the step

scenes.narration: First, an approval is a step you add to a workflow. The run pauses until a workspace owner decides. Wetel never pauses anything for approval on its own.

scenes.title: Every approval needs all three

branches.label: expired
branches.text: Tell the customer someone will follow up

scenes.narration: Every approval step needs three labelled paths. Approved. Rejected. And expired. Wetel refuses to save a workflow that is missing one, so the no answer case always goes somewhere you chose.

scenes.title: Silence is never a yes

items.label: 72 hours
items.text: The default wait

items.label: Up to 14 days
items.text: Set per step

items.label: Then it expires
items.text: A late approve is refused, not acted on

scenes.narration: Silence is never a yes. By default a request waits seventy two hours, and you can set it up to fourteen days. After that it expires, and a late approve is refused, not acted on.

scenes.title: Put something safe on it

items.label: Do
items.text: "I haven't heard back yet. Someone will follow up."

items.label: Don't
items.text: The risky action itself

scenes.narration: So put something safe on the expired path. Tell the customer nobody has decided yet and a person will follow up. Never run the risky action itself. If the step needed a yes, no answer is not a yes.

scenes.title: Test it without waiting

items.label: Draft test
items.text: Simulate approved, rejected or expired instantly

items.label: Notices today
items.text: In-app only. Email is not sent yet

scenes.narration: You can test every outcome in a draft run without waiting. And one honest note: notices are in the app only today. Email is not sent yet.

scenes.title: Human approval, step by step
scenes.subtitle: wetel.dev/docs
scenes.narration: The full walkthrough, from the approval step to the expired path, is in the docs at wetel dot dev slash docs.

title: How much rope should an AI employee get?

scenes.title: Day one. Company card. "Run the business."
scenes.subtitle: Nobody does this to a new hire. So why do it to an AI employee?
scenes.narration: Imagine a new hire's first morning. You hand them the company card and the bank login, and say, run the business, I'll check back in a month. Nobody does that to a person. So why do it to an AI employee?

scenes.title: How much rope?

items.label: 1 · Read
items.text: Look something up. Nothing changes

items.label: 2 · Draft
items.text: A person reads it first

items.label: 3 · Act within limits
items.text: Alone, inside boundaries you set

items.label: 4 · Act after approval
items.text: Money, promises, records

scenes.narration: Autonomy is not one switch, it's a ladder. Reading and looking things up is rung one. Drafting something a person reads first is rung two. Acting alone inside limits you set is rung three. And anything you can't take back waits for approval, on rung four.

scenes.title: Three questions

items.label: Can it be undone?
items.text: A typo, yes. A refund, no

items.label: Who sees it?
items.text: Internal, or a customer

items.label: What does a wrong one cost?
items.text: Once, or forty times

scenes.narration: To place any action on the ladder, ask three questions. Can it be undone? Who sees it? And what does a wrong one cost? You decide the answer in advance, instead of discovering the AI's opinion afterwards.

scenes.title: Don't ask about everything

items.label: Start strict
items.text: Approvals on the consequential steps

items.label: Read the records
items.text: Weeks later, look at what happened

items.label: Loosen with evidence
items.text: Always approved? Move it down a rung

scenes.narration: Won't asking a person slow everything down? Only for the few actions that matter. Start strict. After a few weeks, read the records. If one kind of action is approved every time without edits, move it down a rung.

scenes.title: In Wetel today

items.label: Live
items.text: An approval step you add to a workflow

items.label: Not built yet
items.text: Ask-first as a default policy

scenes.narration: Here is where Wetel stands today. You can add an approval step to a workflow, and it pauses for a workspace owner. But asking first as a default policy is specified, not built.

scenes.eyebrow: Before you hand over the keys
scenes.title: Decide the line in advance
scenes.subtitle: wetel.dev
scenes.narration: So decide the line in advance, per kind of action. The full checklist is on wetel dot dev.

title: When an AI employee fails, what does the customer see?

scenes.title: The warehouse system is down.
scenes.subtitle: What does your customer hear?
scenes.narration: The warehouse system is down, and a customer asks where their order is. What do they hear? That depends on whether someone planned for this moment.

scenes.title: A generic apology

items.label: "Sorry, I ran into a problem"
items.text: What the customer sees

items.label: The real reason
items.text: Kept in the run record, not shown in chat

scenes.narration: By default, if a step fails and nothing catches it, the customer gets a short generic apology. The real reason is not shown in the chat. It is saved in the run record, where you can read it.

scenes.title: Give the step two exits
scenes.narration: For tool and action steps, draw two exits, success and failure. A failure then goes down your branch instead of stopping the run. The error is still recorded, marked as handled, not as an outage.

scenes.title: A bounded loop

items.label: Try again
items.text: The failure edge loops back, up to 3 visits

items.label: Then give up
items.text: A loop exhausted edge hands off

scenes.narration: You can retry a step in a loop with a cap. Say three tries. When the cap runs out, a separate loop exhausted edge takes over with a graceful hand-off. Without that edge, the fourth failure ends in the generic apology.

scenes.title: Make the promise true

items.label: Do
items.text: Say what happens next

items.label: Don't
items.text: Show the technical error

items.label: Only promise a call-back
items.text: If something really arranges one

scenes.narration: Write the failure reply the way a good colleague would talk. Say what happens next. Keep the technical error out of it. And only promise a call-back if something in the workflow actually arranges one.

scenes.title: Plan for the bad afternoon
scenes.subtitle: wetel.dev/docs
scenes.narration: The worked retry example is in the docs at wetel dot dev slash docs.

title: An AI employee that starts on its own

scenes.title: The Monday report nobody asked for.
scenes.subtitle: An AI employee that starts work on its own.
scenes.narration: Every team has that one colleague who sends the Monday report before anyone asks. An AI employee can do the same, with a scheduled workflow.

scenes.title: A timer, not a chat

items.label: Runs the published workflow
items.text: Every weekday at nine, say

items.label: No user message
items.text: Inputs come from the schedule or your systems

items.label: Nobody is waiting
items.text: The workflow must send results outward

scenes.narration: A schedule runs an agent's published workflow on a timer. There is no user message, so inputs come from the schedule's own variables or from your systems. And nobody is waiting, so the workflow has to send its result outward itself.

scenes.title: Three limits

items.label: Plan quota
items.text: How many schedules you may have

items.label: Monthly spend cap
items.text: Checked before every fire

items.label: Auto-disable
items.text: Stops after repeated failures

scenes.narration: Three limits stop it running away. Your plan limits how many schedules you can have. A monthly spend cap is checked before every run. And after repeated failures in a row, the schedule switches itself off.

scenes.title: It stops, but tells nobody

items.label: Today
items.text: No notice is sent when a schedule auto-disables

items.label: So check
items.text: List your schedules, or read the agent activity summary

scenes.narration: One honest gap. When a schedule switches itself off, no notification is sent today. So someone has to check, by listing the schedules or reading the agent's activity summary.

scenes.title: Limits first, then hand it over
scenes.subtitle: wetel.dev/docs
scenes.narration: Set the limits first, then hand it the work. The reference is at wetel dot dev slash docs.

scenes.title: The customer hears "all fixed".
scenes.subtitle: Where is the job sheet?
scenes.narration: A technician finishes a repair. The customer hears, all fixed. But the real proof is the job sheet, the saved account of the work. An AI employee has one too. It's called a run record.

scenes.title: One run, step by step

items.label: Each step, in order
items.text: Only the steps actually visited

items.label: What each produced
items.text: Outputs, requests, errors

items.label: Where it failed
items.text: The real reason, not the apology

scenes.narration: A run record is the saved account of one workflow run. Each step the AI employee visited, in order. What each step produced. And where anything failed, with the real reason, not the generic apology.

scenes.title: One query, three things

items.label: workflowRuns(sessionId)
items.text: Every run of that conversation

items.label: status + errorMessage
items.text: Did it stop, and why

items.label: nodeTrace
items.text: The step list

scenes.narration: You read it with one query, workflow runs, using the conversation's session id. Look at each run's status, its error message, and its step list.

scenes.title: Match the reply to the step

items.label: Said "filed"
items.text: Find the step that sends the application

items.label: Is it in the list?
items.text: A step never reached has no entry

items.label: What did it send?
items.text: Shows it happened, not that it was right

scenes.narration: To check a claim of done, match the reply against the step that should have done the work. If the AI said your application was filed, find the step that sends it. Is it in the list? Did it fail? What did it send? The record shows whether the work happened, not whether it was right.

scenes.title: Read steps, not only status

items.label: Planned failures
items.text: A run can finish normally with a failed step inside

items.label: Secrets
items.text: Masked on a best-effort basis

items.label: Who can read
items.text: Signed-in people in your workspace only

scenes.narration: Two cautions. A planned failure path means a run can finish normally with a failed step inside, so read the steps, not only the status. And secrets are masked on a best effort basis, so never write one into a step's request.

scenes.title: Check what it did, not only what it said
scenes.subtitle: wetel.dev/docs
scenes.narration: The full field guide is in the observability docs at wetel dot dev slash docs.

title: Which AI model does my AI employee use?

scenes.title: Which AI model is it actually using?
scenes.subtitle: And what happens if it fails?
scenes.narration: Which AI model is your AI employee actually using? And what happens if that model fails? Think of a company car pool.

scenes.title: Most trips use the pool car

items.label: Default model
items.text: Used unless someone picks another

items.label: A different car
items.text: For one AI employee or one step

items.label: A spare is sent
items.text: If the default provider fails, a second one is tried

scenes.narration: Most trips use the standard pool car. Your AI employee runs on the platform's default model unless someone picks another. And if a call to the default provider fails, the platform automatically tries a second provider.

scenes.title: Most specific wins

items.label: 1 · The step
items.text: modelOverride on one step

items.label: 2 · The AI employee
items.text: Its own model choice

items.label: 3 · The workspace
items.text: Your workspace's choice

items.label: 4 · The default
items.text: The provider's own

scenes.narration: The most specific choice wins. First the step's own model. Then the AI employee's. Then your workspace's. Then the provider's default. Choosing at the AI employee or workspace level is a pilot today, on request.

scenes.title: Blocked means a clear refusal

items.label: Restrictions
items.text: A Wetel administrator sets them, on your request

items.label: A blocked model
items.text: Refused by name, never silently swapped

items.label: An unknown model on a step
items.text: Fails the run, so check the name before publishing

scenes.narration: Who can restrict models? A Wetel administrator, on your request. If a blocked model is asked for, you get a clear refusal that names it, not a quiet swap. And a step that names an unknown model fails the run, so check the name before you publish.

scenes.title: No speed or quality numbers

items.label: Not published
items.text: Speed or quality figures for any model

items.label: A fallback may differ
items.text: It can answer differently from the default

items.label: So test
items.text: Try it on your own conversations first

scenes.narration: One honest note. We don't publish speed or quality figures for any model, and a fallback model may answer differently. If the choice matters to your work, test it on your own conversations first.

scenes.title: Pick on purpose, not by accident
scenes.subtitle: wetel.dev/docs
scenes.narration: The resolution order and the model catalog are in the docs at wetel dot dev slash docs.

title: Is my company's data kept separate?

scenes.title: Is my data kept apart from other companies'?
scenes.subtitle: Think of an office building with locked floors.
scenes.narration: Is your company's data kept separate from other companies' data? Think of an office building with locked floors. Everyone shares the lifts, but your key card decides which floor the doors open on.

scenes.title: The credential decides

items.label: Dashboard login
items.text: The workspace comes from the token

items.label: API key
items.text: Belongs to one workspace, shown once

items.label: Browser chat token
items.text: One conversation, about an hour

scenes.narration: On every request, the workspace comes from your credential. A dashboard login, an API key, or a short-lived chat token. Never from something the caller types in.

scenes.title: Guessing ids does not help

items.label: Per workspace
items.text: Agents, conversations, knowledge, keys

items.label: Other workspace's records
items.text: Can't be seen or changed, even by guessing numbers

items.label: API keys
items.text: Only a fingerprint is stored, and each can be revoked alone

scenes.narration: A request for one workspace cannot see or change another's data, even if someone guesses record numbers. API keys are shown once, only a fingerprint is stored, and each key can be revoked on its own.

scenes.title: Not in place yet

items.label: Certification
items.text: No third-party security certification yet

items.label: Region
items.text: No choice of where data is stored

items.label: Audit view
items.text: No workspace-wide change log for customers

scenes.narration: Now the honest part. There's no third party security certification yet. No choice of region for where your data is stored. And no workspace wide change log for customers.

scenes.title: Questions worth asking

items.label: Where does the workspace come from?
items.text: The credential, or the caller?

items.label: Who can see our data?
items.text: And exactly what?

items.label: Which parts are live today?
items.text: Roadmap means not available

scenes.narration: Ask any vendor these. Where does the workspace on each request come from? Who on your side can see our data, and exactly what? And if the answer is, it's on the roadmap, treat it as not available today.

scenes.title: Separation you can check
scenes.subtitle: wetel.dev/docs
scenes.narration: The multi tenancy and authentication details are in the docs at wetel dot dev slash docs.

title: When not to use an AI employee

scenes.title: Would you hire a person to add a column?
scenes.subtitle: A buyer's guide that says no.
scenes.narration: You wouldn't hire a person to add up a column of numbers. A calculator does it better. The same goes for an AI employee. Here is when we'd tell you not to use one, even though we build them.

scenes.title: Use a form instead

items.label: Fixed steps, exact numbers
items.text: If it's "if X then Y", write it that way

items.label: Irreversible, and nobody checks
items.text: Keep that action with a person

scenes.narration: First, if the job has fixed steps and exact numbers, a form or a script is cheaper and gives the same answer every time. Second, if a wrong action can't be undone and nobody will check it, keep that action with a person, and let the AI prepare it.

scenes.title: What we haven't built

items.label: Phone calls
items.text: Not built. On the roadmap, not a date

items.label: Memory across conversations
items.text: Not built. Plan it from your own system

items.label: Event triggers
items.text: Not built. Schedules and API calls work

scenes.narration: Third, if you need something we haven't built. Phone calls. Memory from one separate conversation to the next. Or starting work when a record changes in another system. Those are direction, not dates.

scenes.title: Nobody can write it down

items.label: No written process
items.text: "Handle it the way Sarah does" is not a process

items.label: Certification required
items.text: We hold no independent security certification today

scenes.narration: Fourth, if nobody can write the process down, an AI employee won't fix that. Writing it down is the first project, and it doesn't need us. And fifth, if your purchase requires a security certification, we hold none today.

scenes.title: Four signs

items.label: Own words
items.text: People ask in their own words

items.label: Steps on paper
items.text: You can write the steps down

items.label: A named person
items.text: Owns the consequential actions

items.label: Where we connect
items.text: Your site, your app, one messaging app

scenes.narration: It tends to fit when four things are true. People ask in their own words. You can write the steps down. The consequential actions have a named person. And the work arrives where we connect today.

scenes.title: We'll tell you honestly
scenes.subtitle: wetel.dev
scenes.narration: If you're not sure which side of the line your idea falls on, ask us. We'd rather lose a deal than win it on a misunderstanding. Start at wetel dot dev.

title: How an AI employee reads a photo

scenes.title: A customer sends a photo of a parcel label.
scenes.subtitle: What happens next?
scenes.narration: A customer sends a photo of a parcel label. Think of the clerk at a parcel counter. They look at the slip, copy the number, and read the result back. An AI employee does the same job.

scenes.title: One step does the reading

branches.label: fetches
branches.text: Gets the photos from their links

branches.label: saves
branches.text: What it read goes in a variable

scenes.narration: One step in the workflow does the reading. It fetches the photos from their links, shrinks them, sends them to the model, and saves what it read into a named variable. Later steps use that variable like any other text.

scenes.title: How the photo arrives

items.label: A marker in the message
items.text: Your channel writes the image link into the text

items.label: Structured attachments
items.text: Up to 10 per message

items.label: A list in a variable
items.text: For batch jobs and forms

scenes.narration: There are three ways the photo can arrive. A marker in the message text. Structured attachments on the message, up to ten. Or a list of links in a variable, for batch jobs and forms.

scenes.title: Don't let it guess

items.label: Read only what's visible
items.text: Tell it never to infer from file names

items.label: Failed images
items.text: The model is told how many could not load

scenes.narration: Two safeguards. A model can read a word that's only in the file name, so tell it to describe only what is visible. And if some images fail to load, the model is told how many, so it doesn't describe five pictures as if they were all there was.

scenes.title: Check what it read

items.label: Limits
items.text: Up to 40 images, originals up to 20 megabytes

items.label: The run record
items.text: Shows requested, attached and skipped, and why

scenes.narration: The documented limits are up to forty images per step, with originals up to twenty megabytes, shrunk for you. And every run leaves a record that says how many images were requested, attached and skipped, and why.

scenes.title: A photo-reading agent, step by step
scenes.subtitle: wetel.dev/docs
scenes.narration: The photo reading recipe, with the exact configuration, is in the docs at wetel dot dev slash docs.

title: What are credits, and what do they not promise?

scenes.title: Credits are not a prepaid balance.
scenes.subtitle: Think of a company card.
scenes.narration: Credits sound like a prepaid balance. They're not. Think of a company card with a monthly limit and a monthly statement.

scenes.title: What credits are

items.label: A unit for reading usage
items.text: One credit is a ten-thousandth of a US dollar of cost

items.label: Broken down
items.text: By model, operation and bucket

items.label: Your own usage
items.text: One query returns the month's summary

scenes.narration: A credit is a unit for reading your AI usage. One credit is a ten thousandth of a US dollar of underlying cost. Your workspace can see its monthly usage in dollars and credits, broken down by model and operation.

scenes.title: A monthly spend ceiling

items.label: Checked before work starts
items.text: Chat turns, tasks and model calls

items.label: When it's reached
items.text: New work is refused until next month

items.label: A guard, not an exact meter
items.text: Work already running can pass it

scenes.narration: Separately, each plan has a monthly ceiling on language model spend. It's checked before the work starts, and once it's reached, new work is refused until the month rolls over. It's a guard, not an exact meter, so work already under way can carry past it.

scenes.title: Not built

items.label: No prepaid balance
items.text: Nothing stops at zero credits

items.label: No published rate card
items.text: No price per role or per AI employee

items.label: Estimates
items.text: Model credit figures are a blended conversion

scenes.narration: So here is what credits don't promise. There is no prepaid balance, so nothing stops at zero. There is no published rate card, and no price per role. And the credit figures for model usage are an estimate, so plan with them, don't reconcile against them.

scenes.title: What's not charged

items.label: Only the provider that answered
items.text: If one fails and another answers

items.label: Failed tool calls
items.text: Not charged

items.label: A failed run
items.text: Completed steps stay counted

scenes.narration: Two fair details. If one model provider fails and another answers, only the one that answered is billed. And a failed tool call isn't charged. But a failed run isn't refunded, so completed steps stay counted.

scenes.title: Wetel reports usage. It doesn't bill it yet.
scenes.subtitle: wetel.dev/docs
scenes.narration: Today Wetel reports your usage, it doesn't bill it yet. The details are on the pricing page at wetel dot dev slash docs.

title: A model that decides, a workflow that acts

scenes.title: A nurse judges. The hospital acts.
scenes.subtitle: How decision models fit workflows.
scenes.narration: At a hospital triage desk, a nurse looks at you for thirty seconds and says how urgent it is, and which department. Then the hospital takes over. Most AI workflows blur those two jobs.

scenes.title: A chat model as a router

items.label: Asked for one word
items.text: Sometimes it writes a sentence

items.label: No sense of how sure
items.text: A close call looks like a sure one

items.label: Safeguards fix the format
items.text: Not the certainty

scenes.narration: Many workflows ask a chat model for one word, then add code for when it writes a sentence. That fixes the format, not the certainty. A close call gets routed exactly like a sure one.

scenes.title: Three question types

items.label: Yes or no
items.text: A probability, like 0.91

items.label: Choice
items.text: A pick, plus a probability for each option

items.label: Score
items.text: A number on your scale, plus confidence

scenes.narration: A decision model answers closed questions instead of chatting. A yes or no gives a probability. A choice gives a pick, with a probability for every option. A score gives a number on your scale.

scenes.title: Each answer feeds a step
scenes.narration: In Wetel, each answer feeds a step that already exists. A probability goes to a condition with a threshold. A score goes to a switch. A choice goes to a router. The workflow still owns every rule.

scenes.title: Not sure is a path

items.label: The threshold
items.text: Yours to set, from your own examples

items.label: The default edge
items.text: Send it to a person or an approval

items.label: The check
items.text: Try 200 real past messages first

scenes.narration: A person comes in at the threshold, and that number is your decision, not the model's. Point the default path at an approval. Before you trust it, run about two hundred of your own past messages.

scenes.title: Not built yet

items.label: A decision model wired in
items.text: Not built. You would register your own action

items.label: Speed and cost
items.text: Not measured by us yet

items.label: A built-in decision step
items.text: Direction, not a date

scenes.narration: The honest part. No decision model is wired into Wetel yet. The switch and set variable steps are live. We haven't measured speed or cost, and a built in decision step is a direction, not a date.

scenes.title: The full guide is on the blog
scenes.subtitle: wetel.dev
scenes.narration: The full guide is on the Wetel blog at wetel dot dev slash blog. Let a model judge, and let a workflow act.

scenes.title: First come, first served kills.
scenes.subtitle: Triage means sorting under scarcity.
scenes.narration: On a battlefield, treating arrivals in order kills people who could have been saved. So surgeons sort first. Support queues have the same shape, and rarely admit it.

scenes.title: Tiers shield each other

items.label: L0 · Deflect
items.text: Answer from your own docs

items.label: L1 · Sort
items.text: Component, intent, priority

items.label: L2 · Diagnose
items.text: Logs, replication, config

items.label: L3 · Fix
items.text: Code changes, nothing else

scenes.narration: Teams that survive scale end up with tiers. Self-service deflects what never needed a person. Triage sorts the rest. Specialists diagnose. Engineers only ever see code fixes.

scenes.title: Sort, then spend

items.label: 1 · Intake
items.text: Prose into fixed labels

items.label: 2 · Enrich
items.text: Blast radius, past incidents

items.label: 3 · Prioritise
items.text: Impact times urgency

items.label: 4 · Hand off
items.text: Repro, environment, attempts

scenes.narration: Every ticket passes the same four steps. Turn prose into labels. Attach blast radius and past incidents. Prioritise by impact times urgency. Hand off repro steps, environment, and what was already tried.

scenes.title: Impact times urgency

items.label: P1 · Critical
items.text: Down for many

items.label: P2 · High
items.text: Broken, painful workaround

items.label: P3 · Normal
items.text: Minor, one user

items.label: P4 · Low
items.text: Cosmetic or question

scenes.narration: Priority is impact times urgency, never how angry the message sounds. A service down for many customers outranks one angry message, every time.

items.label: Not built yet
items.text: No auto scoring, no SLA timers

scenes.narration: Where Wetel stands today. Classify, route and approval graphs are live, with a run record behind every ticket. But automatic scoring and built-in timers are direction, not built yet.
